change.title: Define software memory and storage limits
change.reason: Current assessment — 2026-11-10, 00c3fe3. Open — all 32 editions still have unknown application workspace; the 80 listed legacy RAM/ROM nulls remain. Approved root narratives preserve these uncertainties rather than supplying measured budgets. Define workspace, installed RAM and ROM applicability separately; an unused ROM may be not applicable, not a missing requirement. Empty-field cleanup is now proposed separately; deleting an explicit null does not establish a known value. Reassess these paths after approval and retain the substantive unknowns in current technical narratives.

before.description: AION Artemis buffered video controller

specification.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of 32 KiB display DRAM. Exclusive 1 KiB sprite SRAM is available in every mode.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

sprites.coordinate_space: Logical mode pixels; scale together with the background. Signed 16-bit X and Y; clip at screen edges.
sprites.priority: Lower sprite number wins; all sprites overlay background/text.
sprites.registers: Two descriptor banks hold signed 16-bit X/Y, enable and reserved controls. CPU/DMA uses auto-incrementing SRAM upload ports.
sprites.allocation_policy: Five sprites in every text/bitmap mode, including double-buffered backgrounds. Sprite SRAM never consumes display DRAM.
sprites.descriptor_allocation_note: 80 bytes of live two-bank descriptors within a 128-byte reserved area; 48 bytes padding. 640 pattern + 128 descriptor + 256 scratch bytes = 1024.

display_memory.organization: 16K × 16 bits; ordinary external DRAM, independent display refresh sequencer.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

specification.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.
specification.monitor_policy: Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

requirements.description: External 16×4116 DRAM and 2×2114 sprite SRAM; integrated 640-byte pixel FIFO and 320-byte row cache. Die-area estimate 80 mm² (60–110), about 65,000–95,000 transistors including SRAM; not a released layout. Qualify timing, large-package pin count, analog-free digital logic and one respin.

chapters.description:
The controller implements {video_link_id} through {display_api_id}. Software selects only modes supported by the controller, monitor profile and available buffer/sprite allocation; unsupported downscaling is rejected.

The corresponding board is {card_id}; external RAM populations below describe that board rather than memory integrated on the die. The controller has a planning die area of {die_area_mm2} mm², not a measured production die.

Display storage is {video_ram_kib} KiB, built from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} devices on a {display_bus_bits}-bit bus. Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of this memory. Sprite storage is independent: {sprite_ram_bytes} bytes from {sprite_chip_count} {sprite_chip_id} chips on a separate {sprite_bus_bits}-bit bus.

One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.

Page selection latches during vertical blank. Double buffering does not guarantee drawing throughput.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

Each bank comprises 40 × 32-bit words and holds 320 pixels, so a 640-pixel line consumes two banks. The renderer expands eight pixels at a time while a separate serializer latch drains ready banks. Underrun blanks pixels and sets a sticky fault.

Two {character_cache_bytes}-byte row caches hold current and next character/attribute rows independently of the pixel FIFO.

The dot clock is {pixel_clock_mhz} MHz. Eight-pixel renderer steps and SRAM latch loads run at {renderer_step_mhz} MHz, rather than requiring one SRAM read per dot. A pixel bank drains in {pixel_bank_drain_us} µs.

Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.

At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

Up to {sprite_count} sprites can appear on each scanline. Each is {sprite_size} pixels at {sprite_bits_per_pixel} bits per pixel, with index {transparent_index} transparent. Lower sprite numbers take priority over higher ones, and all overlay text or background. Signed 16-bit logical coordinates scale with the background and clip at screen edges.

Five patterns occupy 640 bytes. Two banks of 8-byte descriptors use 80 live bytes within a 128-byte reservation, leaving 48 bytes of padding and 256 bytes of scratch space in sprite SRAM. Auto-increment upload ports accept CPU/DMA transfers. Descriptors are banked; patterns are not double-buffered. All sprites remain available when the background is double-buffered.

specification.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of 32 KiB display DRAM. Exclusive 1 KiB sprite SRAM is available in every mode.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

sprites.coordinate_space: Logical mode pixels; scale together with the background. Signed 16-bit X and Y; clip at screen edges.
sprites.priority: Lower sprite number wins; all sprites overlay background/text.
sprites.registers: Two descriptor banks hold signed 16-bit X/Y, enable and reserved controls. CPU/DMA uses auto-incrementing SRAM upload ports.
sprites.allocation_policy: Five sprites in every text/bitmap mode, including double-buffered backgrounds. Sprite SRAM never consumes display DRAM.
sprites.descriptor_allocation_note: 80 bytes of live two-bank descriptors within a 128-byte reserved area; 48 bytes padding. 640 pattern + 128 descriptor + 256 scratch bytes = 1024.

display_memory.organization: 16K × 16 bits; ordinary external DRAM, independent display refresh sequencer.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

specification.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.
specification.monitor_policy: Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

requirements.description: External 16×4116 DRAM and 2×2114 sprite SRAM; integrated 640-byte pixel FIFO and 320-byte row cache. Die-area estimate 80 mm² (60–110), about 65,000–95,000 transistors including SRAM; not a released layout. Qualify timing, large-package pin count, analog-free digital logic and one respin.
Define the external video RAM bus, arbitration, scan timing, font path and output serializers/drivers; qualify the package against the buffered controller design.
PCB dimensions, layer stack, finish, connectors, fitted passives and reference designators
Power per rail, startup/thermal limits and region-specific power configuration
Firmware image capacity/revision, programming and verification
Assembly routing, test fixtures, cycle times, yield/rework/scrap and packout

chapters.description:
The controller implements {video_link_id} through {display_api_id}. Software selects only modes supported by the controller, monitor profile and available buffer/sprite allocation; unsupported downscaling is rejected.

The corresponding board is {card_id}; external RAM populations below describe that board rather than memory integrated on the die. The controller has a planning die area of {die_area_mm2} mm², not a measured production die.

Display storage is {video_ram_kib} KiB, built from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} devices on a {display_bus_bits}-bit bus. Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of this memory. Sprite storage is independent: {sprite_ram_bytes} bytes from {sprite_chip_count} {sprite_chip_id} chips on a separate {sprite_bus_bits}-bit bus.

One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.

Page selection latches during vertical blank. Double buffering does not guarantee drawing throughput.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

Each bank comprises 40 × 32-bit words and holds 320 pixels, so a 640-pixel line consumes two banks. The renderer expands eight pixels at a time while a separate serializer latch drains ready banks. Underrun blanks pixels and sets a sticky fault.

Two {character_cache_bytes}-byte row caches hold current and next character/attribute rows independently of the pixel FIFO.

The dot clock is {pixel_clock_mhz} MHz. Eight-pixel renderer steps and SRAM latch loads run at {renderer_step_mhz} MHz, rather than requiring one SRAM read per dot. A pixel bank drains in {pixel_bank_drain_us} µs.

Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.

At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

Up to {sprite_count} sprites can appear on each scanline. Each is {sprite_size} pixels at {sprite_bits_per_pixel} bits per pixel, with index {transparent_index} transparent. Lower sprite numbers take priority over higher ones, and all overlay text or background. Signed 16-bit logical coordinates scale with the background and clip at screen edges.

Five patterns occupy 640 bytes. Two banks of 8-byte descriptors use 80 live bytes within a 128-byte reservation, leaving 48 bytes of padding and 256 bytes of scratch space in sprite SRAM. Auto-increment upload ports accept CPU/DMA transfers. Descriptors are banked; patterns are not double-buffered. All sprites remain available when the background is double-buffered.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign
before.objective: Encourage independent manufacturers and developers to adopt documented compatibility interfaces, and show customers how supported software, documents and peripherals can protect their investment across computer brands.
message: Choose your computer. Keep your investment.
Use documented interfaces and qualified configurations to connect products from independent suppliers.
Choose CP/M applications, FlexiBUS peripherals and display options separately; adopting one does not require the entire Logix platform.
Prepare for future computers through portable C source and documented interfaces while continuing to use and support established eight-bit systems.
audience: Business customers choosing computers, applications and peripherals.
Independent computer and peripheral manufacturers evaluating compatibility programmes.
Software publishers, developers, dealers and integrators supporting existing and future systems.

marketing_steps.description: Qualify partner claims and protect the next-generation architecture disclosure.

marketing_presentation.description: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not change software ownership or imply open-source licensing. Reference-code rights, certification scope and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, future-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.
Do not imply an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

marketing_steps.description: Demonstrate independent customer choices at NCC 1979.

marketing_presentation.description: Allow {programme_minutes} minutes for the presentation programme; questions and follow-up are separate.
Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Explain how independent software, peripheral and display choices can protect a customer’s investment.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Demonstrate an Abacus document round trip between Aurelia and the Model II prototype using separately qualified host editions. Show supported common behaviour without promising identical binaries or disk formats.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Demonstrate Abacus, then independent SSG General Ledger records and summary export. Explain the prepared data and separate licensing; do not imply that SSG has a Model II port.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Operate a qualified peripheral sequentially on named hosts. Show identification, driver support and supported application functions, attaching only when the port is quiescent.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Present the Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II alongside the S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative joins the native Apple demonstration. Explain the drivers, optional display hardware and separate S-100 support without suggesting Apple endorses S-100 systems.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, SSG management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. {presenter} explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

Allow {duration_minutes} minutes for this block. Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_steps.description: Explain the separate software, peripheral and display compatibility profiles.

marketing_presentation.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.
Explain implementation and qualification requirements for {subject}.
Explain supported interaction behaviour under {subject}.
Present {subject} to developers implementing supported interfaces.
Explain source portability through {subject}, with recompilation and testing still required.
Distinguish graphics API compatibility under {subject} from qualified display hardware.
Explain the qualified monitor connection defined by {subject}; this is not a consumer television interface.

marketing_steps.description: Recruit independent implementers under explicit terms and governance.

marketing_presentation.description: Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and scope, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

marketing_steps.description: Explain source migration, legacy support and the continuing eight-bit market.

marketing_presentation.description: The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television. A computer intended to use an existing television requires separate display engineering; the basic-storage configuration remains unresolved.

marketing_steps.description: Qualify partner claims and protect the next-generation architecture disclosure.

marketing_presentation.description: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not change software ownership or imply open-source licensing. Reference-code rights, certification scope and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, future-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.
Do not imply an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

marketing_steps.description: Explain the separate software, peripheral and display compatibility profiles.

marketing_presentation.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.

specification.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of 32 KiB display DRAM. Exclusive 1 KiB sprite SRAM is available in every mode.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

display_memory.organization: 16K × 16 bits; ordinary external DRAM, independent display refresh sequencer.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

specification.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.
specification.monitor_policy: Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

assembly_requirements.description: Engineering baseline; electrical qualification, routing and supplier quotes pending.

requirements.description: Dedicated slot; powered-off replacement only; host interface, power rails and signal integrity require qualification.
Qualification pending.

chapters.description: The card uses {graphics_controller_id} and implements {video_link_id} through {display_api_id}. Software selects only modes supported by the controller, monitor profile and available buffer/sprite allocation; unsupported downscaling is rejected.

Display storage is {video_ram_kib} KiB, built from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} devices on a {display_bus_bits}-bit bus. Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of this memory. Sprite storage is independent: {sprite_ram_bytes} bytes from {sprite_chip_count} {sprite_chip_id} chips on a separate {sprite_bus_bits}-bit bus.

One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.

Page selection latches during vertical blank. Double buffering does not guarantee drawing throughput.

Sprite geometry and compositing follow {sprite_protocol_id} {sprite_profile}.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

Each bank comprises 40 × 32-bit words and holds 320 pixels, so a 640-pixel line consumes two banks. The renderer expands eight pixels at a time while a separate serializer latch drains ready banks. Underrun blanks pixels and sets a sticky fault.

Two {character_cache_bytes}-byte row caches hold current and next character/attribute rows independently of the pixel FIFO.

The dot clock is {pixel_clock_mhz} MHz. Eight-pixel renderer steps and SRAM latch loads run at {renderer_step_mhz} MHz, rather than requiring one SRAM read per dot. A pixel bank drains in {pixel_bank_drain_us} µs.

before.description: Logix Artemis 64 KiB video controller card

specification.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: With palette-list mode enabled reserve 0xFA00–0xFFFF (1536 bytes); framebuffer/text/font allocations use 0x0000–0xF9FF. Text/font and bitmap layouts remain exclusive. Five sprites retain separate 1 KiB SRAM.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

display_memory.organization: Two 16K x 16-bit banks; ordinary DRAM, not dual-port VRAM. Preserve independent refresh and bounded host access.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: Requalify existing renderer/FIFO and 16-bit DRAM organization for 640x400x2 and 640x200x4, refresh, sprite fetches, list prefetch and host/DMA stalls together. No greater upload throughput is promised by added capacity.

specification.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.
specification.monitor_policy: All earlier modes and sprite/host/API features retained subject to monitor capabilities. Color Pro 14 and Mono Pro support the 640x400 raster; older displays retain their declared raster limits. Horizontal-retrace palette lists require explicit monitor capability; otherwise use static/vertical-retrace palette updates. No forced high scan rate on old monitors.

technical_definition.athena_qualification: Existing card baseline selected; Athena host electrical/firmware compatibility remains a release gate.

assembly_requirements.description: Engineering baseline; electrical qualification, routing and supplier quotes pending.

requirements.description: New controller, 64 KiB DRAM decoding, palette sequencer and host/DMA arbitration require timing, power and release qualification.

chapters.description:
The card uses {graphics_controller_id} and implements {video_link_id} through {display_api_id}. Software selects only modes supported by the controller, monitor profile and available buffer/sprite allocation; unsupported downscaling is rejected.

It extends {previous_card_id}; {palette_list_id} adds scanline palette changes.

Display storage is {video_ram_kib} KiB, built from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} devices on a {display_bus_bits}-bit bus. Two 16K × 16-bit banks use ordinary DRAM, not dual-port VRAM. Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of this memory. Sprite storage is independent: {sprite_ram_bytes} bytes from {sprite_chip_count} {sprite_chip_id} chips on a separate {sprite_bus_bits}-bit bus.

When palette lists are enabled, reserve 0xFA00–0xFFFF (1536 bytes); text, fonts and framebuffers occupy 0x0000–0xF9FF.

One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.

Page selection latches during vertical blank. Double buffering does not guarantee drawing throughput.

Sprite geometry and compositing follow {sprite_protocol_id} {sprite_profile}.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

Each bank comprises 40 × 32-bit words and holds 320 pixels, so a 640-pixel line consumes two banks. The renderer expands eight pixels at a time while a separate serializer latch drains ready banks. Underrun blanks pixels and sets a sticky fault.

Two {character_cache_bytes}-byte row caches hold current and next character/attribute rows independently of the pixel FIFO.

The dot clock is {pixel_clock_mhz} MHz. Eight-pixel renderer steps and SRAM latch loads run at {renderer_step_mhz} MHz, rather than requiring one SRAM read per dot. A pixel bank drains in {pixel_bank_drain_us} µs.

Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.

Requalify existing renderer/FIFO and 16-bit DRAM organization for 640x400x2 and 640x200x4, refresh, sprite fetches, list prefetch and host/DMA stalls together. No greater upload throughput is promised by added capacity.

All earlier modes and sprite/host/API features retained subject to monitor capabilities. Color Pro 14 and Mono Pro support the 640x400 raster; older displays retain their declared raster limits. Horizontal-retrace palette lists require explicit monitor capability; otherwise use static/vertical-retrace palette updates. No forced high scan rate on old monitors.

Use on {planned_base_computer_athena} and {planned_base_computer_athena_server} requires electrical and firmware qualification; selection of the existing baseline does not establish that these hosts are ready.

Requalify existing renderer/FIFO and 16-bit DRAM organization for 640x400x2 and 640x200x4, refresh, sprite fetches, list prefetch and host/DMA stalls together. No greater upload throughput is promised by added capacity.

All earlier modes and sprite/host/API features retained subject to monitor capabilities. Color Pro 14 and Mono Pro support the 640x400 raster; older displays retain their declared raster limits. Horizontal-retrace palette lists require explicit monitor capability; otherwise use static/vertical-retrace palette updates. No forced high scan rate on old monitors.

Use on {planned_base_computer_athena} and {planned_base_computer_athena_server} requires electrical and firmware qualification; selection of the existing baseline does not establish that these hosts are ready.

chapters.description:
Logix Aurelia — base computer is a slim desktop built around {processor_id}.

The {expansion_bus_bits}-bit expansion interface supports Plug and Execute. Connector space is reserved for a future 32-bit interface; that is not current bus width.

Installed RAM must satisfy the selected configuration, and a monitor must connect to a fitted video provider. Cartridges must match both the software platform and their socket role; external application cartridges are supported.

The {memory_model_id} maps {lower_ram_kib} KiB of lower RAM plus {common_ram_kib} KiB of fixed common RAM at F000–FFFF. The normal 48 KiB view maps RAM at 0000–AFFF and ROM/cartridge/video windows at B000–EFFF. {expansion_card_id} extends lower RAM to 60 KiB by supplying B000–EFFF, reaching the 64 KiB system limit. Within 7000–EFFF, 4 KiB pages may temporarily expose ROM or video RAM; hidden RAM retains its contents and is restored after service calls.

The {system_controller_id} refreshes every installed bank independently of CPU activity and latches physical DMA bank selections so mapping changes cannot redirect a transfer. The base population uses {ram_bank_count} 8-bit banks, with common RAM included and no parity. Mixed module types are not allowed.

Motherboard ROM contains {firmware_services}. The {video_controller_id} operates display RAM on an independent 8-bit bus; sprite RAM has a further separate 8-bit bus.

{recommended_system_id} supplies the native Z80/CP/M environment. Applications use {application_api_id} and query usable dimensions rather than branching on model names. Native 40 × 25 and 80 × 25 text are available subject to monitor capabilities.

inputs.description: The founders held an organising meeting on 30 January 1982. It provides the date basis and preparatory context for the agreement signed on 31 January, which starts this funded development programme. The source does not identify the meeting attendees.
Native AIONix/ERA build with reliable floating-point geometry and typed coordinate entry
Dual-display driver with colour command/status screen and 800x600 drawing canvas; independent palettes and explicit input focus
Explicit CAD mouse integration; standard TUI mouse support alone is insufficient
Drawing load/save and DXF exchange tests against the other supported AutoCAD builds
Supported pen-plotter output and physical drawing verification
Measured RAM, storage, redraw and stability requirements on the qualified configuration; backup/restore and reproducible release build
Feature baseline agreed with Autodesk; no automatic import of later AutoCAD dimensioning, object-snap or 3D features

team environment / workstations: Supply an Artemis PRO with 1 MiB RAM, local storage and available display to each assigned developer, plus shared build/test and spare machines as the agreed staffing plan requires. No invented fixed team size.

team environment / software: Install the entire AION Development System — Team Edition: C Development Environment 2, ERA compiler/linker/debugger and validated floating-point math library; source repository, branches/reviews, tasks, collaboration, reproducible builds, release labels and target testing.

team environment / network: Supply network adapters, hub, cabling, configured accounts and project permissions, and dedicated Artemis PRO server capacity. Scale sponsored server/license deployments to the whole team within qualified concurrency; the retail four-session entitlement is not silently unlimited.

team environment / storage: The standard 5 MB disk is inadequate as a presumed whole-team repository/build archive. Fund and qualify larger storage, additional volumes/servers, independent backup media, restore tests and off-machine source archives; capacities follow measured source/build/history budgets.

team environment / support: Fund dedicated Autodesk engineering time, AION compiler/runtime and integration specialists, installation, training, documentation, replacement hardware, plotter access and on-site support through release. Retail onboarding/support-hour caps do not limit this separately sponsored agreement.

team environment / early graphics: January work uses available Artemis PRO displays and a stable software implementation of the graphics API. Supply 64 KiB/Color Pro engineering samples and mouse prototypes when qualified; do not make January work depend on the June professional hardware.

team environment / professional handover: Around June 1982 deliver the 128 KiB professional card and Logix Mono Pro 17 to the development and QA team, alongside the 64 KiB colour card/Color Pro 14 and mouse. This supersedes the earlier proposed January 17-inch prototype handover.

funding: Adam commits to supplying the staffing, equipment, licences and integration resources required by the agreed delivery plan. No arbitrary dollar ceiling or fabricated cost estimate; procurement and staffing are reviewed against the November objective.

outcomes.description: Deliver AutoCAD 1.0 for Artemis/AIONix for the joint November 1982 COMDEX presentation; November release-quality build is the commitment, with commercial shipment subject to acceptance rather than automatically deferred to December.

Qualify the professional display interfaces required by the November CAD configuration, including inherited modes, palette sequencing and five-sprite compatibility. Preserve the separate June development handover; CAD development does not create the underlying graphics technology.

steps.description: Deliver AutoCAD 1.0 for Artemis/AIONix for the joint November 1982 COMDEX presentation; November release-quality build is the commitment, with commercial shipment subject to acceptance rather than automatically deferred to December.
Meet programme acceptance gates; commercial shipment remains conditional on acceptance.

After incorporation on 26 April 1982, Autodesk adopts the founders' development arrangement, confirms source/porting rights and non-exclusive licensing, and reviews the compiler, recovery and graphics-driver milestones.
Milestone during this process: Professional 800x600 hardware becomes available to Autodesk.

before.title: Ecosystem growth and market response — CP/M / 8-bit era
before.description: CP/M / 8-bit ecosystem development from July 1978 through the portable-system competition milestone on 1 April 1981. Build the ecosystem of independent manufacturers, software developers and peripheral contributors around Aurelia’s CP/M with TUI, FlexiBUS, C development interfaces, graphics subsystem and digital monitor connectivity. Coordinate documented implementation and qualification, SMC second-source transfer, portable DRI extensions and Tandy cooperation. CP/M activity continues alongside the Artemis ecosystem phase; the envelope does not imply universal adoption or completion of all later targets.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign — execution
before.description: Prepare the compatibility programme and partner demonstrations, deliver the NCC 1979 presentation and expansion-product launch, then run recruitment, dealer activity and qualification follow-up through the January 1980 review. Campaign.ncc1979 supplies the messages, presentation and marketing materials.

inputs.description: The Aurelia launch provides the working platform and business applications used to prepare cross-vendor demonstrations.
The Tandy cooperation agreement provides the basis for the Model II prototype and application-interchange work.
The limited Apple cooperation agreement provides documentation, test machines and compatibility assistance for native Apple II products.

Prepare named configurations, host-specific drivers, documented transfer paths and measured resource limits. Protect future architecture information and clear partner participation before public demonstrations.

outcomes.description: Published compatibility profiles, implementation guidance and records of unresolved access and support terms.
Rehearsed demonstration configurations, interoperability test records and an issue register distinguishing verified behaviour from limitations.
The NCC presentation and expansion-product launch have been delivered, with native Apple and S-100 support described separately and partner responsibilities retained.

An updated compatibility directory, recruitment and qualification records, dealer and developer materials, and an evidence-based closing review. Adoption and sales targets are not treated as achieved outcomes.

steps.description: Evaluate recruitment prospects and engineering kits. Prioritise North Star, with Lifeboat as a possible integration or distribution partner, then Vector Graphic. Preserve existing applications and display investment; interest does not constitute an agreement.

Treat North Star and Vector as strong CP/M prospects with moderately strong FlexiBUS prospects; optional Logix video is a moderate fit for North Star and a lower fit for Vector. Cromemco is a moderate CP/M and FlexiBUS prospect but a weak Logix-video prospect because of its own OS and graphics strategy. Altos is a moderately strong CP/M prospect with moderate FlexiBUS and limited Logix-video potential; no platform redesign is assumed. Intertec has moderately strong CP/M and moderate host-specific FlexiBUS potential, with limited Logix-video interest; plan late-1979 evaluation and possible 1980 qualification, not June availability. Heath/Heathkit has moderate CP/M and host-specific FlexiBUS potential but limited Logix-video interest; treat it as later feasibility work, not a promised 1979 release. These assessments guide outreach and do not establish commitments.
Publish compatibility profiles and provide reference-driver and test access alongside the separate DRI extension release. Record unresolved commercial and support terms.

Prepare the presentation space, audiovisual equipment and qualified demonstration systems. Test document round trips, disk formats, memory limits, loading, recalculation and device behaviour. Review all public material for the embargo and secure partner clearance.
Run supplier workshops, test named configurations and record failures and required corrections before public demonstrations.
Deliver the NCC presentation and the combined Apple II/S-100 expansion-product launch using the approved campaign materials and qualified systems.
Run dealer demonstrations, joint trade-press activity and developer clinics. Maintain a directory that distinguishes shipping, qualified and prototype configurations.
Review progress against the campaign’s adoption targets using verified OEM configurations, qualifications and third-party device availability.

Track compatible-computer sell-through across vendors, qualified application editions, peripheral shipments and supported device classes, document-interchange results, support incidents, supplier concentration and component availability. Count distinct manufacturers rather than duplicate dealer builds or SKUs.

Prepare the closing review with verified customer examples, compatibility results and partner configurations. Report progress toward NCC 1980 goals without claiming unverified results or disclosing future architecture.

before.title: NCC 1982 — Pointy ideas with a solid point. — execution
before.description: Introduce mouse-driven business workflows, colour upgrades and recreational mouse tutorials; support the public presentation with dealer preparation, press briefings, developer clinics and measured follow-up.

inputs.description: Demonstrations require tested colour and mouse configurations, compatible software builds and clear application update paths. Availability and qualification must be established before each public demonstration.

outcomes.description: Public introduction of the colour and mouse offerings, with dealer demonstrations and customer follow-up. This is a marketing result; product design and manufacture are established outside campaign execution.

Publication and demonstration of the CP/M and AIONix pointing updates. Standard TUI controls gain mouse activation; static libraries require relinking and custom interfaces require adaptation. This release activity does not create the operating systems.
Release and public demonstration of the CP/M and AIONix Entertainment Suite implementations with mouse-learning tutorials, keyboard alternatives and monochrome-compatible presentation.

steps.description: Prepare dealer and Academy demonstrations at the opening milestone.
Brief press and partners and rehearse the public presentation.
Open the public presentation at the Astrodomain in Houston on 7 June; continue conference demonstrations through 10 June.
Hold developer clinics and partner compatibility sessions.
Conduct regional demonstrations, enquiry handling and upgrade follow-up.
Publish customer case studies and review the campaign results.

before.description: Abacus 1.x (CP/M edition)

portability_contract.shared_logic: Separate application/document algorithms from platform adapters.
portability_contract.display: Query dimensions and attributes; use semantic colors and clipping.
portability_contract.memory: Bounded buffers and handles for banked objects; report allocation failures.
portability_contract.storage: Versioned, explicitly encoded records; no persisted pointers or raw C structures.
portability_contract.migration: Recompile for the target, adapt OS-specific modules and test resource limits. This does not expand the listed supported platforms.

data_interchange.contract: Import versioned SSG General Ledger summary files into ordinary worksheet cells as independent planning inputs. Map named columns, account identifiers, period, currency and decimal amounts; reconcile control totals. Validate parsing, rounding, memory and save/reopen. Close General Ledger before loading Abacus. The import is handled by Abacus itself and requires no scripting runtime, formatted-table object or report-layout engine. There is no direct ledger write-back, live database link or simultaneous application execution.

chapters.description: Abacus 1.x stores one sparse worksheet per document, with formulas and editor-consistent navigation and editing. Its initial scope is worksheet calculation and printing worksheet results. Formatted table/report layouts and scripting integration belong to later releases.

Abacus imports versioned disk summaries from {accounting_export_id} into ordinary worksheet cells as independent planning inputs. Map named columns, account identifiers, period, currency and decimal amounts, then reconcile record counts and control totals. Validate parsing, rounding, memory limits and save/reopen. Close General Ledger before loading Abacus; there is no ledger write-back, live database access or simultaneous application execution. This built-in import does not depend on a scripting runtime, formatted-table object or report-layout engine.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

This application suite targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. It requires {runtime_cpm_aurelia}. The edition is delivered on diskette. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

chapters.description:
Abacus 3 is the native 32-bit Artemis spreadsheet and analysis line. Sparse worksheets and schema-defined formatted-table tabs coexist with multiple tabs, cross-tab references, typed columns, virtual calculated columns, unique-key lookups and a documented read-only SQL subset. Disk-backed columnar storage uses column pruning, conservative statistics-based skipping and dataset-dependent encoding rather than promised compression or throughput.

Reports extend earlier spreadsheet-field layouts with one-off/repeating sections and graphical {chart_types} charts. Capability-aware preview includes titles, axes and legends while retaining standard TUI editing and monochrome patterns. Supported printer drivers paginate output; refresh stale query/formula results before printing.

Embedded Pulse uses the Abacus-owned document API; standalone Pulse retains exclusive offline access to supported closed files. Preserve formulas and invalidate changed cached results rather than allowing a second concurrent writer.

Versioned SSG summaries remain independent planning inputs with decimal checks and reconciliation, without ledger write-back or a live database link. CSV import maps schemas, quoting, delimiters, encodings, dates, decimal conventions, nulls and text identifiers, with rejected-record diagnostics. Value-only export explicitly loses formulas and types.

VSAM import consumes host-exported sequential logical records, for example through IDCAMS REPRO, with a supplied record layout and transfer path. Declare boundaries, lengths, offsets and keys; convert EBCDIC, supported binary, packed decimal and zoned decimal explicitly. Raw VSAM images, clusters and indexes are not desktop interchange files. Reject unsupported layouts without reinterpretation. Preserve older document versions; older Abacus/Pulse editions must reject unsupported new features before writing.

The initial release uses flat formatted tables. Bounded nested arrays/maps/structs with explicit aggregation/expansion and broader Lotus 1-2-3 response features are later work. It does not promise background recalculation, unlimited documents/memory, a full transactional SQL database, arbitrary VSAM image access or unrestricted nested data.

Qualify actual Artemis 128/256 KiB and later PRO configurations separately. Measure memory, storage, timing, I/O and compression on named datasets; larger jobs may need expansion or disk-backed processing. Exercise sales import, customer/product joins, margins, regional grouping, printed charts, save/reopen and the equivalent Pulse script. Check conversions, rounding, nulls, duplicate keys, join cardinality, cancellation, grouped undo, visibility, dependency invalidation, recovery and unsupported-version rejection. No unmeasured minimum RAM or maximum row count is asserted.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

chapters.description:
AIONix2 develops {baseline_os_id} for {processor_architecture_id}, retaining {portable_api_id}. The initial release combines executable system ROM, documented legacy ABI compatibility, protected preemptive user processes, recoverable HDD storage, users/permissions, a POSIX-oriented subset and an event-driven TUI foundation.

ROM execution/ABI, resilient multitasking and recoverable storage are essential, followed by access enforcement and the staged interface/UI work. Paging, metadata journaling, broader networking, threads/locales and a full windowed GUI remain later work, not initial release gates. These are engineering priorities rather than completed qualification.

Stable kernel code, core libraries, a small shell/basic utilities and recovery tools share read-only, cacheable executable ROM; each process keeps writable state in DRAM. The replaceable system cartridge supplies at least {minimum_os_rom_bytes} bytes. EEPROM BIOS remains boot/diagnostic firmware; optional services, larger utilities and patches load from disk rather than copying the entire ROM into RAM.

Executable ABI versions select legacy adapters, stable library dispatch and capability discovery. Preserve documented ERA instruction semantics, C calling conventions and layouts, syscall entry/numbers, loading, errors and legacy signals. Privileged drivers, undocumented kernel assumptions and direct hardware access need separate qualification; Z80 C code must be recompiled. Versioned dispatch and page-sized RAM overlays patch code after ROM checksum/version checks, with recovery boot bypassing disk patches. A qualified minor revision can be installed by exchanging a host-compatible cartridge.

The preferred DRAM allocation is {preferred_dram_bytes} bytes; the 256 KiB minimum is an engineering fit target, not a measured guarantee, and the server retains its existing 1 MiB configuration. Illustrative allocations are 40 KiB for kernel state/tables/stacks, 24 KiB for filesystem buffers, 16 KiB for translation metadata, 12 KiB for terminal/UI input, 20 KiB for services/patch reserve and 144 KiB for applications. Shared ROM, sparse page tables, small kernel stacks and reliable copy-on-write reduce demand. Allocation failure must be handled; ROM cannot replace writable RAM. Later swap requires qualified restart, locking and I/O with fault handlers resident, and should address occasional pressure rather than routine oversizing.

A compact monolithic kernel timer-preempts user processes while bounding non-preemptible kernel critical sections. Priority aging, sleeping I/O and atomic sleep/wakeup provide fairness; short interrupts defer work. Validate user pointers, protect kernel/device mappings, constrain per-process memory/files/requests, bound driver retries and timeouts, and retain responsive administrative termination. Process exit cleans files, memory, locks and child state. Kernel-controlled DMA uses checked pinned buffers; process isolation alone protects neither kernel/driver faults nor DMA. A fully preemptible kernel and application threads are not initial requirements.

A versioned inode filesystem separates directory entries from metadata, using {allocation_block_bytes}-byte blocks and {block_identifier_bits}-bit block IDs. The initial qualification range is {qualification_volume_mb} MB, not a capacity ceiling or bundled-drive change. Direct/indirect pointers, metadata timestamps/link counts, bounded caches, mounts and logical-sector drivers with CHS translation support the layout.

Clean/dirty state, a consistency checker, ordered metadata writes, explicit synchronization and tested backup/restore establish recoverability. Exact disk format/limits, file-offset and timestamp representation, legacy import/mount behaviour and controller persistence guarantees remain open. A later small metadata journal still needs power-loss/write-order testing and does not alone ensure application-data durability.

Numeric users/groups, owner/group/other permissions including directory search, creation masks, real/effective credentials and login/home directories define access. Protect salted, costed password hashes within CPU budgets and enforce permissions on every relevant kernel operation. Device/mount/configuration administration and audit records are protected. Qualify credential/exec transitions before enabling set-user-ID programs; servers authenticate users rather than trusting supplied UIDs. Extended ACLs are later work.

The initial subset defines file/descriptor operations and errors; descriptor duplication/inheritance; copy-on-write fork, exec, wait, status and environment; signals/masks/dispositions and interruption; canonical/raw terminals and foreground process groups; hierarchical paths, working directories and hard/symbolic links; pipes, EOF/broken-pipe handling and readiness multiplexing; shell quoting, redirection, pipelines, variables and statuses; wall and monotonic clocks with explicit timestamp formats. Publish an implemented/partial/absent matrix and unsupported-operation errors rather than claiming conformance from names. Efficient spawn, broader file control/mapping, full job control/pseudo-terminals, sockets/IPC, utilities, locales, threads and timers are later additions.

Applications own business logic and semantic Open/Save/Select/Cancel commands. A shared abstraction provides events, menus, forms, lists, focus, layout, measurement and drawing contexts; translation adapters preserve TUI, terminal, device and legacy ABI behaviour above native process/file/IPC/timer/input/display services. These are logical library/service layers, not four mandatory processes or IPC hops.

A bounded event queue handles keys, timers, focus, redraw and future pointer events. Opaque view/window handles initially describe text regions; clipping, invalidation, repaint, layout constraints and text measurement use separate cell/pixel coordinates. Clipboard/selection ownership is bounded, and graphics/font/colour/pointer support is discovered by version and capability. Compact text state, dirty regions and redraw callbacks avoid a mandatory full-screen backing bitmap. A later GUI can host old character applications in terminal windows without automatically redesigning them.

Release tests must cover legacy binary regressions, fairness/termination under CPU load, injected faults and cleanup, concurrent disk/terminal/DMA I/O, power loss and durable saves, credentials/permissions, measured ROM/RAM use with Abacus/compiler/server workloads, and TUI fallback/legacy terminal behaviour.

This operating system targets native ERA/AIONix on {host_base_computer_athena} and {host_base_computer_athena_server}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified beyond the explicit system-ROM requirement.

Efficient spawn, broader file control/mapping, full job control/pseudo-terminals, sockets/IPC, utilities, locales, threads and timers are later additions.

Applications own business logic and semantic Open/Save/Select/Cancel commands. A shared abstraction provides events, menus, forms, lists, focus, layout, measurement and drawing contexts; translation adapters preserve TUI, terminal, device and legacy ABI behaviour above native process/file/IPC/timer/input/display services. These are logical library/service layers, not four mandatory processes or IPC hops.

A bounded event queue handles keys, timers, focus, redraw and future pointer events. Opaque view/window handles initially describe text regions; clipping, invalidation, repaint, layout constraints and text measurement use separate cell/pixel coordinates. Clipboard/selection ownership is bounded, and graphics/font/colour/pointer support is discovered by version and capability. Compact text state, dirty regions and redraw callbacks avoid a mandatory full-screen backing bitmap. A later GUI can host old character applications in terminal windows without automatically redesigning them.

Release tests must cover legacy binary regressions, fairness/termination under CPU load, injected faults and cleanup, concurrent disk/terminal/DMA I/O, power loss and durable saves, credentials/permissions, measured ROM/RAM use with Abacus/compiler/server workloads, and TUI fallback/legacy terminal behaviour.

This operating system targets native ERA/AIONix on {host_base_computer_athena} and {host_base_computer_athena_server}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified beyond the explicit system-ROM requirement.

chapters.description:
The system adapts {base_version} for banked-ROM execution while preserving standard entry points, loading conventions and available-memory boundaries. A single foreground application can use ordinary CP/M console/file services; richer behaviour uses the separate versioned Logix API.

The CCP interprets commands and loads disk/cartridge programs; BDOS supplies file services through the machine BIOS, which adapts calls to Logix drivers. Motherboard ROM supplies {firmware_contents}. The system cartridge supplies {cartridge_contents}; command buffers and mutable system state remain in RAM. ROM constants/code must be separated from state and self-modifying routines adapted.

In conventional CP/M, 0000H–00FFH holds vectors, default file-control data and the command/disk buffer. Programs load at {program_load_address} in the transient program area and call BDOS through {bdos_entry}; CCP, BDOS and BIOS occupy higher memory. The TPA is application RAM, not an OS module. Transient editor/copy/assembler/debugger/maintenance utilities load when needed.

Compared with 1.3, the 1.4 base supports four logical drives, BIOS sector translation and extra drive state; BDOS begins one 256-byte page lower while CCP/BIOS bases stay fixed. It revises disk errors, returns DE consistently with HL and splits BDOS into PL/M logic plus an assembly interface. Vanilla 1.4 does not contain Logix banked-ROM, cartridge, dynamic-driver, TUI/clipboard/workspace services or the later CP/M 2.0 disk-parameter-block model.

Logix boot firmware discovers cartridges and provides diagnostics/recovery. The common-memory runtime preserves accessible entry code, stack and interrupt state across nested bank switches, following {memory_model_id}. Drivers in motherboard/device ROM or extensions register video, keyboard, floppy and FlexiBUS services. BIOS and relevant BDOS assumptions must match Aurelia disk formats. DMA uses physical-bank descriptors, bounded transfers and ready handshakes; drain or abort it before warm boot or buffer reuse. Video uploads expose dedicated sprite SRAM and atomic descriptors with backpressure, falling back to programmed I/O where needed.

chapters.chapter_name: Shared TUI ownership and application behaviour
chapters.description:
The system owns {tui_contract_id}, exposed through {portable_api_id} and {display_api_id}. It supplies reusable controls, while {consumer_business_tools_aurelia}, {consumer_abacus_1}, {consumer_abacus_2}, {consumer_ssg_general_ledger} and {consumer_pulse_1} retain their document, calculation, file-management and scheduling logic.

Screen services query usable dimensions, clip/scroll and distinguish document from display coordinates. Compact 40-column and expanded 80-column layouts fit dialogs, names and errors; semantic text/selection/warning roles map to colour or monochrome. Structured character, function/navigation and modifier events support blocking or polled input. Shared fields, lists, menus, forms, popups and focus movement use consistent editing and clipboard commands. Clipboard formats, lengths, capacity, ownership and errors are explicit. Contexts are created/destroyed and activated/deactivated with redraw; one may cover the whole screen. System timing and repeat replace CPU-speed loops.

Sequential applications can use these services without multitasking. Exact widgets, clipboard capacity and workspace reservations remain implementation choices. Preserve legacy console behaviour and stable target ABI, use capability discovery, and avoid hard-coded stride, video addresses, last columns or hardware registers. The same documented API spans Aurelia, Aurelia+ and Artemis; Artemis mediates shared display/clipboard access between processes.

This operating system targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.
