implementation_design.title: SSG General Ledger transactional client/server v1
implementation_design.architecture: Thin Z80/ERA clients send bounded business operations to an Artemis PRO server. Query evaluation, indexes, validation, accounting posting and transactions execute on the server; clients do not fetch arbitrary database pages.

transactions.concurrency: Single serialized writer for v1 with short transactions and bounded reader locks; no long interactive transaction while a user edits a form.
transactions.commit: Append checked log records and a commit marker, force them to durable storage, then acknowledge. Apply/replay committed changes idempotently.
transactions.recovery: On startup validate checksums and recover committed log records; incomplete transactions never become visible. Use shadow page/index replacement or another explicitly validated torn-write-safe method.
transactions.failure: Do not claim durable commit until disk/controller completion semantics are proven; no battery-backed cache is assumed.
transactions.log_format: Redo-only changed-record/page after-images with transaction ID, sequence, length and checksum; the commit marker covers transaction record count and checksum. Persist duplicate-suppression outcomes in the same transaction.
transactions.buffer_policy: Do not write uncommitted changes to database files (no-steal); cap transaction size to available transaction buffers.
transactions.checkpoint: Write replacement pages and indexes to new locations, force them, then alternate checksummed generation-numbered root/checkpoint records. Retain the preceding valid root and necessary redo log until the new checkpoint is durable.

protocol.transport: Length-framed requests over TCP; bounded messages and chunked results.
protocol.duplicate_suppression: Store committed write request IDs and outcomes durably. After reconnect, clients query status or retry with the same ID; never post the same journal twice.

data_integrity: Amounts use explicitly scaled integers/decimal rules, never unspecified binary floating-point rounding.
Record currency, rounding, posting dates, account periods and unique document IDs.
Journal and balance posting is atomic and produces an append-only audit record.
operations: Backup captures a consistent checkpoint plus required logs; test restoration onto a clean disk.
Bounded log growth, disk-full handling and operator-visible recovery status
Plan backups and report traffic around the negotiated shared 100/250/500/1000 kbit/s raw LAN budget and measured payload throughput; slower admitted hosts limit the whole network.

initial_limits.client_policy: Bounded pages of results and forms; no entire-table download or whole-document duplication.

acceptance_tests: Concurrent journal postings and account inquiries
Full disk, corrupt log tail and failed backup restore

distribution.network_operation: Start under the existing networking OS, connect to server, and load further modules/data over the network; bootstrap remains local.
distribution.data_access: Business transactions, validation and database writes remain server-side; clients do not directly modify shared database files.

chapters.description: The scope is SSG General Ledger journals, balances, queries and reports. This edition sends bounded business operations to the relational accounting service on {server_host_id} running {server_edition_id}. Queries, indexes, validation, posting and transactions stay server-side; clients receive bounded pages of forms/results rather than arbitrary database pages or whole tables. {network_stack_id} supplies the network path. Robustness and capacity remain acceptance targets.

Version 1 serializes writers with short transactions and bounded reader locks; editing a form must not hold an interactive transaction open. Redo after-images carry transaction ID, sequence, length and checksum; a commit marker covers record count and checksum. Force log and commit marker to durable storage before acknowledging, then apply/replay changes idempotently. Persist request IDs and outcomes in the same transaction so a lost acknowledgement can be retried without posting a journal twice.

Uncommitted data must not reach database files; transaction size is limited by buffers. Checkpoint into replacement pages/indexes, force them, then alternate checksummed generation-numbered roots. Retain the previous valid root and required redo log until the new checkpoint is durable. Startup validates checksums and exposes only committed work. Torn-write safety and disk/controller completion semantics must be proven; no battery-backed cache is assumed.

Length-framed TCP requests use {request_fields}. Operations are {operations}; messages and streamed results are bounded. Reconnecting clients query status or reuse the original durable request ID.

Amounts use explicit scaled-integer/decimal rules with currency, rounding, posting dates, periods and unique document IDs. Journal and balance postings are atomic and append an audit record. Backups capture a consistent checkpoint and required logs, with restoration tested on a clean disk. Bound log growth, handle full disks and expose recovery status.

The server target is {server_ram_kib} KiB with {concurrent_sessions_target} concurrent sessions. Plan backups/reports around the negotiated shared 100/250/500/1000 kbit/s raw LAN budget and measured payload throughput; the slowest admitted host limits the common rate. Test power loss around acknowledgements, duplicate retries, concurrent postings, disk-full/corrupt-log failures, backup restoration and a 48 KiB Aurelia client.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

This client targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. It requires {runtime_cpm_aurelia_networking}. A local startup diskette boots the client under its existing networking OS before bounded transfers load further modules or data. This edition is supplied as part of its containing package. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

Business Tools supplies a text editor, disk browser, calculator and calendar/scheduler. Each application owns its documents, calculations or records while calling system screen, editing, list, form, clipboard and file services.

Reusable widgets, input/screen primitives, clipboard ownership and workspace entry/return belong to {system_tui_id}. The application cartridge keeps its own logic and avoids a second shared TUI library. It retains a 16 KiB physical capacity and one cartridge position alongside the system cartridge; removing duplicate code does not establish a measured free-space budget. Code can execute from banked ROM while writable state and any resident workspace consume explicitly reserved RAM; residence does not imply multitasking.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

This application suite targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. It requires {system_tui_id}. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

before.name: AION C IDE (CP/M edition)
before.description: AION C IDE 1.0 for Aurelia enhanced CP/M: an integrated syntax-highlighting editor, project build workflow, optimizing Z80 C compiler, assembler/linker, debugger and tuned runtime libraries. Shared ROM TUI bindings and SDK helpers support keyboard-operated forms and data controls; capability-based drawing supports text and bitmap modes. Tools run sequentially with overlays as required by the 48/64 KiB profiles.

features: Core C runtime and target-specific optimized libraries
Shared Logix C/TUI/graphics headers and target libraries

Integrated source editor with lexical syntax highlighting for C keywords, comments, strings, character literals and preprocessor lines; selection and diagnostics remain distinguishable on color and monochrome monitors.
Incremental recoloring of affected visible lines, bounded multiline-comment state and disk-backed source editing; no full semantic language server or requirement to hold an entire project in RAM.
Project source/module list, include paths, library selection, size/speed/debug profiles, incremental rebuilds and compiler-error navigation; source and cursor state survive sequential tool execution.

Optimizing Z80 backend: constant folding/propagation, dead and unreachable code elimination when provably safe, local common-expression elimination, redundant load/store removal, branch simplification and target-specific peephole optimization.

Basic-block liveness and register-pair allocation; loop address induction and strength reduction where profitable, with conservative treatment of aliases, external calls, signed arithmetic and hardware access.
Selective small-function inlining when a definition is available, balanced against code growth; no promised whole-program optimizer or universal speed multiplier.

Optimized assembly library kernels for block copy/fill, string scan/compare, integer arithmetic, selected decimal/fixed-point operations and record comparison/search; documented numeric precision, rounding, overflow and errors.

Link only referenced library modules. Use optimized routines at useful granularity, measuring call and ROM-bank overhead; benchmarks compare identical workloads and correctness, not unsupported claims of assembly-equivalent performance.

Forms with text fields, bounded lists, tables, dropdown selection and buttons. SDK helpers compose existing ROM TUI controls where a native service is absent; tables use row callbacks or bounded visible pages rather than copying an entire dataset.

Tab and Shift-Tab focus traversal, documented keyboard shortcuts, copy/cut/paste through the system clipboard, consistent selection/editing and validation. Controls have explicit buffer lengths, ownership, error and event semantics.

Text and bitmap drawing bindings: discover usable modes, clip, draw text/glyphs, lines, rectangles/fills and transfer documented bitmap formats. A bitmap control renderer shares control state and keyboard semantics, with application-linked helper code where required.

Applications redraw from document state after mode changes. Text and bitmap modes share video RAM; no simultaneous full-screen buffers, universal 80-column mode, guaranteed bitmap speed or automatic conversion of legacy applications.

User-supplied Z80 assembly modules and libraries link with C objects using a published ABI, symbol convention and object/archive format; examples cover C-to-assembly calls, assembly-to-C calls and safe callbacks.

Assembly interfaces document arguments/returns, preserved registers, stack balance, integer/pointer sizes, layout, clobbers and reentrancy. ROM-call stubs preserve banks/stacks; interrupt code must not reenter non-reentrant OS/TUI services.

Debug builds retain source/line-to-address maps where emitted, symbol inspection and RAM breakpoints/single-step. Optimized instructions may not map one-to-one to source; ROM code is debugged through supported stubs or qualified RAM-loaded equivalents.

Measure tool overlays, editor buffers, optimizer intermediates, stack, system workspaces and disk scratch usage on 48/64 KiB hosts; resource requirements are qualification gates and no measured throughput or fit is invented.

chapters.description: AION C IDE integrates source editing, project/module configuration, compilation, assembly, linking, diagnostics and debugging. The editor highlights C keywords, comments, string/character literals and preprocessor lines using semantic attributes. Monochrome displays use distinguishable supported intensity/inverse attributes; selection and error emphasis remain readable. Lexical recoloring is restricted to affected visible text with bounded state for multiline comments. Disk-backed buffers support sources larger than editor working memory. Tools may execute sequentially and use overlays, preserving source, cursor and diagnostic state.

The compiler implements {language_contract_id} and libraries follow {runtime_contract_id}. Structures, typedef, function pointers, documented 32-bit integer arithmetic and shared string/stream-I/O semantics are retained. Profiles {build_profiles} build {build_targets}; later ANSI C features and future processor targets are not implied. The project records modules, include paths, libraries and debug/size/speed options, rebuilds changed modules and maps diagnostics back to source locations.

The Z80 optimizer performs constant folding and propagation, provably safe dead/unreachable-code elimination, local common-expression elimination, redundant load/store removal, branch simplification and target-specific peephole optimization. Basic-block liveness and register-pair allocation reduce memory traffic. Loop address induction and strength reduction are used when profitable; small visible function bodies may be selectively inlined under size/speed policy. Aliasing, external/assembly calls, signed arithmetic and hardware effects constrain transformations. Driver calls and declared hardware accesses are treated as observable effects. Assembly interface declarations must expose clobbers and side effects or the compiler assumes conservative barriers. No full modern whole-program optimizer is promised. Compare optimized and unoptimized outputs for identical numeric and I/O behaviour.

Performance-critical block copying/filling, string scanning/comparison, integer arithmetic, selected decimal/fixed-point operations and record comparison/search kernels are implemented in tuned Z80 assembly. Publish operation widths, precision, rounding, overflow, overlap and error rules. Link only referenced library modules; application data and writable runtime state remain in RAM. Users can assemble their own modules, create libraries and link them with C objects. Publish symbols, object/archive format, argument/return locations, preserved registers, stack rules, data layout and callback/reentrancy requirements. Supply C-to-assembly, assembly-to-C and callback examples. Interrupt handlers do not reenter non-reentrant CP/M/TUI routines. Benchmark useful operations including call and bank-switch overhead; no blanket speed or code-size guarantee.

Headers, ROM-call stubs and examples use the accepted system-cartridge TUI. Provide text fields, lists, tables, dropdown selection and buttons with consistent validation, Tab/Shift-Tab focus traversal, keyboard shortcuts, selection and copy/cut/paste. DRI owns shared clipboard storage/lifecycle; helpers obey published capacity, formats and ownership. The IDE SDK supplies composite table/dropdown helpers over existing ROM primitives when a native control is absent; this does not silently add new services to the accepted ROM image. Tables request bounded rows/pages through application callbacks. Forms use C-defined descriptors and callbacks; a visual drag-and-drop form designer is not part of this release.

Use {display_api} to enumerate/test/select modes and query the actual configuration. Text mode is the compact default for the IDE; generated applications can draw text/glyphs, lines, rectangles, fills and documented bitmap formats with clipping. SDK adapters render the same control model in text or bitmap mode with shared keyboard semantics; optional helper code links into the application rather than assuming every renderer is in ROM. Bitmap rendering is limited to qualified modes and memory budgets. Mode changes preserve application document/control state and trigger redraw. Do not assume simultaneous text and full bitmap buffers, readable 80 columns on every monitor, transparent conversion of old programs or hardware drawing acceleration.

Provide symbol maps, emitted source/line-to-address mappings, inspectable RAM state, RAM breakpoints and single-step for qualified builds. Optimized code may reorder or remove source operations; use debug builds for predictable stepping. XIP ROM cannot be patched with software breakpoints: use supported call stubs or qualified RAM-loaded equivalents. ROM-aware linking separates code/constants from initialized and uninitialized RAM data, provides disk/cartridge images and reports ROM/RAM usage and stack estimates. Indirect calls, recursion and assembly routines can prevent a proven stack bound and must be flagged.

Supported hosts are {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}, using {runtime_cpm_aurelia}; the nominal installed-RAM minimum remains {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The 48 KiB profile publishes 40704 application bytes and the 64 KiB profile 57088 bytes under the existing reservations. These are ceilings, not spare space available to every tool. Measure editor buffers, pass overlays, library state, stack and disk intermediate files against actual reservations. A single-drive workflow may require media exchanges. Two distribution diskettes follow the recorded package definition, with image fit, working-disk requirements and installation qualification still required. No additional RAM or ROM capacity is inferred.

Qualify syntax coloring and recovery from unterminated comments/strings, diagnostic navigation, incremental builds, library selection, C/assembly calls and nested bank restoration. Compare debug/optimized arithmetic and file results; test overlap, rounding, overflow and invalid inputs. Exercise forms and bitmap redraw in 40/80-column and monochrome/color configurations, clipboard-full, disk-full and exhausted-memory failures. Benchmark forms/record entry, sorting/search, decimal accounting and a bounded recalculation workload on named hardware. Report executable size, peak workspace, stack estimates, disk scratch use and build/run times. Fast libraries and advanced optimization are implementation commitments; measured superiority to earlier tools or hand-written assembly remains to be demonstrated. SSG General Ledger is an external acceptance workload: reconcile CBASIC and C financial results, measure native application work and ROM TUI overhead separately, and keep the publisher’s source and accounting rules outside the reusable IDE product.

compatibility_policy.eligibility: Any manufacturer or independent integrator may implement the published environment without a bespoke partnership or mandatory certification.
compatibility_policy.binary: Existing Z80 binaries require compatible instruction execution and the specified OS/runtime and memory behaviour; CP/M alone is insufficient. Other processors need an appropriate port or execution solution.
compatibility_policy.hardware: Native video, keyboards, disks and printers may be exposed through adapters. FlexiBUS and Logix video hardware are separate optional profiles. Full hardware clones may implement those published interfaces under their applicable terms.
compatibility_policy.applications: Named supported platforms are tested configurations, not an exclusive permission list. Independently implemented environments may run properly licensed applications; certification identifies precisely what AION tested.
compatibility_policy.delivery: Printed manuals/source listings and disks; host/media conversion quoted separately.
compatibility_policy.certification: Optional, configuration- and version-specific. Manufacturer-declared compatibility is distinct from AION-tested application compatibility. FlexiBUS electrical/protocol and Logix display tests are separate claims.

chapters.description:
The kit documents released 8-bit Aurelia processor, CP/M, memory, display, keyboard, storage and error-behaviour contracts. It supplies runtime-adapter source and redistribution terms, diagnostics and failure/resource-limit tests, plus Abacus/Business Tools workloads for calculation, interchange, printing and save/reopen. Manuals, source listings, machine-readable disks and versioned result forms support independent implementations.

Any manufacturer or integrator can implement the environment without a bespoke partnership or mandatory certification. Existing Z80 binaries need compatible instructions and OS/runtime/memory behaviour; CP/M alone is insufficient, and another processor needs a port or execution solution. Native video, keyboard, disk and printer interfaces may use adapters; FlexiBUS and Logix video are separate optional profiles, including applicable terms for hardware clones.

Named supported platforms are tested configurations, not an exclusive permission list for properly licensed applications. Optional certification applies to an exact configuration/version and distinguishes a manufacturer’s claim from AION-tested application compatibility; FlexiBUS electrical/protocol and Logix display claims are separate. Printed documentation/source listings accompany disks; host/media conversion is a separate delivery requirement.

before.name: FlexiBUS
before.description: FlexiBUS

specification.description: FlexiBUS provides {Communication}. Devices support identification and can be attached dynamically while the bus is inactive. Before normal operation, the host reads the peripheral ROM metadata: {Peripheral ROM metadata}.

parameters.value: DEVICE ID, DEVICE TYPE, VENDOR, PROTOCOL VERSION, POWER REQUIREMENTS

specification.description:
The technical specification is published for third-party implementation. Manufacturers can build non-exclusive, independently branded devices; adopting Logix software or video is optional. Logix commits to forward peripheral compatibility across future computer generations, using the published contracts, including {Keyboard standard reference} for keyboard behaviour.

Plotter, modem and specialist classes still need designed and qualified profiles and drivers. Discovery metadata alone does not establish that a device works.

DRI leads the software interfaces, Logix contributes hardware specifications, and independent manufacturers participate. The final governance charter, fees and support period remain open.

Each host port connects to one device through separate differential transmit and receive pairs using asynchronous serial framing. The v1 topology does not support passive multidrop connections or implicit daisy chains.

Supported raw rates are {Supported rate (bps)} bps. A port starts at {Startup rate bps} bps. The cable target is a shielded connection up to 3 m at 500 kbit/s, subject to signal-integrity testing and qualification of period-appropriate line components.

The electrical drawing must define the power contacts, current limits and keyed connector pinout. Disk and printer devices are self-powered; keyboard power is current-limited.

Attach or detach a device only while its port is quiescent. Ground-first contacts and power sequencing must be specified; the design does not claim unrestricted live hot-plugging.

Messages use 8N1 byte transport, a 0x7E delimiter, and escaping for delimiter and escape bytes. The header contains {Header}, followed by a payload of at most {Max payload bytes} bytes.

CRC-16-CCITT protects the unescaped header and payload. Its polynomial is {CRC polynomial}, its initial value is {CRC initial value}, and its final XOR value is {CRC final XOR}; reflection is disabled. The wire specification must fix byte order before implementation.

Initially, each device can have one outstanding request. Explicit ACK/NAK responses, bounded timeouts and retries, a BUSY indication and response credit provide flow control.

parameters.value: protocol version, message class, flags, request ID, payload length

specification.description:
The command set includes {Commands}. Sequence and request identifiers prevent duplicate execution; the device retains its last completed request and response until the session resets. A write retry carries the same identity, and a media change invalidates queued requests.

Reset starts a new session epoch. If a non-idempotent operation such as printing has an uncertain outcome, report that uncertainty rather than silently retrying it. Removal, CRC errors, timeouts and unsupported operations are reported through stable OS errors.

Disk devices buffer complete sectors locally, so host throughput need not match the raw disk bit rate. With 8N1 framing, {Fast link rate} permits at most {Fast link ceiling}, and {Slow link rate} permits at most {Slow link ceiling}, before headers, escaping and turnaround. Keyboard polling must not monopolise the CPU during disk transfers.

Device descriptors and class protocols are architecture-neutral. The host OS supplies Z80 or ERA class drivers. Any optional device-specific ROM driver must identify its ISA and ABI explicitly; a Z80 ROM driver must never be executed as ERA code.

parameters.value: IDENTIFY and capabilities; RESET and health; Keyboard event read; Printer status and bounded output blocks; Disk geometry/media generation, sector read/write and flush

specification.description: Qualification must exercise the host and peripheral together. Check FIFO overrun and worst-case CPU service latency, printer backpressure, disk retry after a lost reply, CRC faults, cable removal and power sequencing. These are required tests, not a statement that qualification has already passed.

after.name: FlexiBUS peripheral standard
after.description: Shared peripheral transport, discovery and device-class contracts; pointing devices are a later optional class, not another core standard.

specification.description: FlexiBUS v1 defines the peripheral transport used at the Aurelia launch on 5 June 1978. The January 1975 agreement is a development commitment, not proof of release. Independent compatibility programmes are explicitly published on 5 May 1979; wider publication and new host implementations do not establish a new transport version. The pointing-device class is introduced with the NCC presentation on 7 June 1982 and uses the existing transport. It is not part of the 1978 baseline and does not imply unrestricted hot-plugging. Transport requirements, class extensions and measured implementation qualification remain distinct. TUI owns user-facing keyboard and pointer meanings.

specification.description:

The {Primary card memory} card occupies the existing dedicated video slot; the {Professional card memory} professional card occupies one general {Expansion bus width} expansion slot. The accelerator supports bounded drawing operations while vector geometry remains authoritative. Damage redraw, line quality and memory limits govern the rendering strategy.

before.name: LogixLAN negotiated-rate physical and data-link standard
before.description: LogixLAN negotiated-rate physical and data-link standard

specification.description:
Stations connect through an active hub over {Cable} using {Connector}. The hub grants one transmitter at a time; this baseline is a shared network rather than independent switched links.

Hub-controlled polling grants transmit access to one station at a time, avoiding collision-detection hardware.

Stream the granted frame to other admitted ports at the common rate; destination filtering and CRC validation occur in adapters. No independent per-port rates, frame-store switching or rate conversion in the 1981 baseline.

Simple, deterministic and inexpensive LAN implementation using technology comfortably available by 1981.

The network forms an active star through a multiport hub, repeater and arbiter.

Balanced differential serial signalling is compatible in principle with EIA-422-class line drivers and receivers.

Cable pairs have distinct roles: pair 1 carries station-to-hub differential data; pair 2 carries hub-to-station differential data; pair 3 carries the hub-distributed synchronous clock and transmit-grant timing; pair 4 is reserved for diagnostics or later expansion.

HDLC-inspired bit-oriented frames contain address and control fields and a 16-bit frame check sequence.

The adapter stores or configures a locally assigned link address; broadcast is supported.

Supported raw rates are {Supported rates kbps} kbit/s. Startup and fallback use {Startup rate kbps} kbit/s. Every admitted station shares the same negotiated rate, and host qualification constrains advertised capabilities.

One common rate across all admitted stations; one transmitter at a time. Port count does not multiply shared bandwidth. Application throughput is lower and remains unvalidated.

The stable logix_lan100_link identifier is retained for references; 100 denotes the mandatory startup/fallback rate, not the maximum rate.

Each listed host requires qualification.

The fallback rate is {Fallback rate kbps} kbit/s; the maximum shared raw rate is {Maximum shared raw rate kbps} kbit/s. Host qualification covers {Qualified host}.

The hub selects the highest rate supported by every admitted station and link. Changes are coordinated through acknowledgements, a quiet switch interval and test frames; failures return to the startup rate.

Intersection of adapter hardware capability, firmware-enforced host qualification ceiling and configured cable/reliability limits. Platform ceilings are design qualification targets, not measured throughput claims.

Hub selects the highest rate in the intersection of its own capability and every admitted station/link capability. A 100-only station or link limits the whole network to 100 kbit/s.

Choose the highest common candidate; announce a switch epoch and bounded idle interval at 100 kbit/s and collect acknowledgments from all admitted stations.

Drain the current frame and stop grants before changing the distributed clock. Do not switch with a missing acknowledgment.

Run bounded test frames on every admitted link at the candidate rate; resume normal grants only after every link passes.

On failed qualification or persistent link errors, return to 100 kbit/s for coordination, exclude the failed candidate and try the next lower common rate. If 100 fails, isolate the faulty port and report the fault.

Periodically drain traffic and open an announced 100 kbit/s discovery window. New stations join only after coordinated renegotiation; admitting a slower station lowers the common rate. Discovery windows consume shared bandwidth.

Adapters use a timeout independent of the distributed bit clock. On lost clock/control or switch timeout, stop transmitting and await the hub at 100 kbit/s. The hub watchdog restores 100 kbit/s and a new negotiation epoch; never allow unilateral station transmission at a different rate.

Reset/start at 100 kbit/s; keep unadmitted ports isolated from normal traffic.

Poll station identity, supported-rate bitmap, host profile and receiver capacity at 100 kbit/s.

Adapters offload framing and buffer complete frames. The local packet RAM target is {Adapter requirements local packet RAM target bytes} bytes, separate from host RAM. Receiver credit controls admission of complete frames before transmission.

Local adapter RAM, additional to host system RAM. Partition transmit/receive buffers and metadata; freeze maximum frame length and IP MTU to fit complete frames before implementation. Physical RAM chip count remains unresolved.

Grant unicast only when the destination advertises credit for a complete frame; reserve that credit until completion. Broadcast requires credit from all intended admitted receivers. Timeouts revoke stale credits; bounded queues and retry/error reporting prevent indefinite blocking. Use flow control first for receiver pressure, not automatic rate changes.

No per-byte interrupt requirement. Aurelia at {Aurelia link rate} has {Aurelia CPU budget} per raw byte at {Aurelia CPU clock}; Aurelia+ at {Plus link rate} has {Plus CPU budget} at {Plus CPU clock}. Validate worst-case service latency. A persistently slow host may advertise a lower configured ceiling.

Hub clock-divider reference only; does not require every adapter or host logic path to run at 10 MHz.

Adapters must provide serial framing and CRC generation/checking.

Adapters must provide destination filtering before CPU interrupt.

Adapters must provide complete-frame buffering.

Adapters must provide packet-level interrupts and receiver-ready reporting.

The hub uses the ordered clock-divisor choices {Clock generation bit clock divisors} for the supported rates. These divisors belong to the hub clock reference, not to every host logic path.

parameters.key: Adapter requirements local packet RAM target bytes

specification.description:
Timing, buffer limits, recovery and mixed-host throughput require measurement. The qualification checks below must pass before advertised rates become delivery claims.

Mixed-platform admission, missing acknowledgments, clock loss, buffer exhaustion and broadcast backpressure.

Qualification must cover cable lengths, termination, drivers and clock skew at each advertised rate.

Qualification must cover exact frame format/length, IP MTU, buffer partitions and credit accounting.

Qualification must cover discovery cadence, switch/ack timeouts and independent recovery watchdog.

Qualification must cover error thresholds, test-frame counts and fallback hysteresis.

Qualification must cover sustained TCP/IP throughput and CPU load on all four host platforms.

The stable logix_lan100_link identifier is retained for references; 100 denotes the mandatory startup/fallback rate, not the maximum rate.

Each listed host requires qualification.

The fallback rate is {Fallback rate kbps} kbit/s; the maximum shared raw rate is {Maximum shared raw rate kbps} kbit/s. Host qualification covers {Qualified host}.

The hub selects the highest rate supported by every admitted station and link. Changes are coordinated through acknowledgements, a quiet switch interval and test frames; failures return to the startup rate.

Intersection of adapter hardware capability, firmware-enforced host qualification ceiling and configured cable/reliability limits. Platform ceilings are design qualification targets, not measured throughput claims.

Hub selects the highest rate in the intersection of its own capability and every admitted station/link capability. A 100-only station or link limits the whole network to 100 kbit/s.

Choose the highest common candidate; announce a switch epoch and bounded idle interval at 100 kbit/s and collect acknowledgments from all admitted stations.

Drain the current frame and stop grants before changing the distributed clock. Do not switch with a missing acknowledgment.

Run bounded test frames on every admitted link at the candidate rate; resume normal grants only after every link passes.

On failed qualification or persistent link errors, return to 100 kbit/s for coordination, exclude the failed candidate and try the next lower common rate. If 100 fails, isolate the faulty port and report the fault.

Periodically drain traffic and open an announced 100 kbit/s discovery window. New stations join only after coordinated renegotiation; admitting a slower station lowers the common rate. Discovery windows consume shared bandwidth.

Adapters use a timeout independent of the distributed bit clock. On lost clock/control or switch timeout, stop transmitting and await the hub at 100 kbit/s. The hub watchdog restores 100 kbit/s and a new negotiation epoch; never allow unilateral station transmission at a different rate.

Reset/start at 100 kbit/s; keep unadmitted ports isolated from normal traffic.

Poll station identity, supported-rate bitmap, host profile and receiver capacity at 100 kbit/s.

Adapters offload framing and buffer complete frames. The local packet RAM target is {Adapter requirements local packet RAM target bytes} bytes, separate from host RAM. Receiver credit controls admission of complete frames before transmission.

Local adapter RAM, additional to host system RAM. Partition transmit/receive buffers and metadata; freeze maximum frame length and IP MTU to fit complete frames before implementation. Physical RAM chip count remains unresolved.

Grant unicast only when the destination advertises credit for a complete frame; reserve that credit until completion. Broadcast requires credit from all intended admitted receivers. Timeouts revoke stale credits; bounded queues and retry/error reporting prevent indefinite blocking. Use flow control first for receiver pressure, not automatic rate changes.

No per-byte interrupt requirement. Aurelia at {Aurelia link rate} has {Aurelia CPU budget} per raw byte at {Aurelia CPU clock}; Aurelia+ at {Plus link rate} has {Plus CPU budget} at {Plus CPU clock}. Validate worst-case service latency. A persistently slow host may advertise a lower configured ceiling.

Hub clock-divider reference only; does not require every adapter or host logic path to run at 10 MHz.

Adapters must provide serial framing and CRC generation/checking.

Adapters must provide destination filtering before CPU interrupt.

Adapters must provide complete-frame buffering.

Adapters must provide packet-level interrupts and receiver-ready reporting.

The hub uses the ordered clock-divisor choices {Clock generation bit clock divisors} for the supported rates. These divisors belong to the hub clock reference, not to every host logic path.

specification.description:
Timing, buffer limits, recovery and mixed-host throughput require measurement. The qualification checks below must pass before advertised rates become delivery claims.

Mixed-platform admission, missing acknowledgments, clock loss, buffer exhaustion and broadcast backpressure.

Qualification must cover cable lengths, termination, drivers and clock skew at each advertised rate.

Qualification must cover exact frame format/length, IP MTU, buffer partitions and credit accounting.

Qualification must cover discovery cadence, switch/ack timeouts and independent recovery watchdog.

Qualification must cover error thresholds, test-frame counts and fallback hysteresis.

Qualification must cover sustained TCP/IP throughput and CPU load on all four host platforms.

change.title: Define the Plug and Execute compatibility contract before classifying it as a standard
change.reason: The current record states automatic ROM identification/configuration but does not sufficiently specify independently implementable connector, discovery, driver ABI, resource allocation and conformance rules. Retain its current interface kind pending a concrete contract and chronological scope.

findings.description: Determine the common expansion contract versus platform-specific implementations and establish its availability from existing story evidence. Do not assume all generations share a connector, ABI or already-qualified capability.
